medium.title: Boletus edulis
medium.line: Species of mushroom, widely distributed in the Northern Hemisphere

medium.text: Boletus edulis is a basidiomycete fungus, and the type species of the genus Boletus.

medium.caption: The fruit body has a large brown cap which can reach 30 cm in diameter and 3 kg in weight.

events.label: Early alternate names include Boletus solidus by English naturalist James Sowerby in 1809.
The French-born King Charles XIV John popularised B. edulis in Sweden after 1818.
A similarly sized specimen found in Poland in 2013 made international news.

medium.text: The fungus produces spore-bearing fruit bodies above ground in summer and autumn.
B. edulis is also one of the few fungi sold pickled.

deep.title: Boletus edulis
deep.line: Species of mushroom, widely distributed in the Northern Hemisphere

deep.text: Boletus edulis is a basidiomycete fungus, and the type species of the genus Boletus.

deep.caption: The fruit body has a large brown cap which can reach 30 cm in diameter and 3 kg in weight.

events.label: Early alternate names include Boletus solidus by English naturalist James Sowerby in 1809.
The French-born King Charles XIV John popularised B. edulis in Sweden after 1818.
A similarly sized specimen found in Poland in 2013 made international news.

deep.text: Boletus edulis was first described in 1782 by the French botanist Pierre Bulliard and still bears its original name.
A 1987 revision of the International Code of Botanical Nomenclature set the starting date at May 1, 1753, the date of publication of Carl Linnaeus’ Species Plantarum.
The cap of this mushroom grows up to 8–30 cm wide, sometimes more.
The stipe grows up to 8–25 cm tall and 2–7 cm thick—rather large in comparison to the cap.
The undersurface of the cap consists of thin tubes, the site of spore production; they are 1 to 2 cm deep, and whitish in colour when young, but mature to a greenish-yellow.
Viscid when moist, the cap is convex when young and flattens with age.
B. edulis is also one of the few fungi sold pickled.
